text: What is the practical difference between `final int x = 1;` and `final int[] a = {1};`?
choices: `final` prevents reassignment of the array reference and also fixes the array's length.
`final` forbids rebinding the name in both cases, so `x` cannot change but `a[0]` can.
`final` on a primitive is a compile-time constant, while on an array it has no effect at all.
`final` on an array makes its contents immutable as well, so neither can change.
explanation: `final` constrains the arrow, never the thing at the end of it. That distinction is why Chapter 20 has to argue for immutability as a design discipline rather than as a keyword — a `final` field holding a mutable object gives you no guarantee at all about what the object holds, and defensive copying exists precisely to close that gap.
